metaDescription: Honeywell HPA5300, HPA3100, HPA304, HPA4300, HHT270 and Air Genius 5 compared by room size, filter type, auto mode and upkeep before you choose one.
expertTake: The HPA5300B is the pick for big rooms and the HPA3100 is the dependable mid-size choice for most homes. The Allergen Plus HPA4300W is the one to buy if you want sensor-driven auto mode and easy filter changes, and the Air Genius 5 suits people who hate buying filters. Anyone who needs strong odor removal should look at heavier carbon machines.
introParagraphs: Mainstream purifier families tend to split into three groups: small tabletop units, mid-size towers and big floor models. The differences are less about technology than about how much air the fan moves and how the filters are changed.
That is the lens to use here. Matching the machine's size class to your room and its filter style to your patience will matter more than any single feature on the box.

products.name: Honeywell HPA5300B extra-large room HEPA purifier
products.description:
The HPA5300B is the biggest of the HPA family listed here and is aimed at open living areas and large bedrooms. It uses a HEPA filter with a carbon pre-filter, plus an air quality indicator and an auto mode that watches the room and changes fan speed.

The auto mode is the real convenience. A sensor-driven fan will idle on a clean day and speed up when you cook or vacuum, which a manual machine never does without your help. The carbon pre-filter is a light layer, so it softens everyday smells but will not tame heavy smoke odor. Versus the HPA3100 it moves more air and costs more to feed.

Upkeep is a washable or replaceable carbon pre-filter and a HEPA filter that is changed on the maker's schedule. Because the unit is large, give it clear floor space and avoid pushing it tight to a wall.
products.bestFor: Open living areas and large bedrooms that want auto mode.
pros: Extra-large room class with strong airflow
Auto mode adjusts fan speed to the air
HEPA plus carbon pre-filter
Air quality indicator is easy to read
cons: Carbon pre-filter is light for heavy odors

products.name: Honeywell PowerPlus HPA3100 HEPA purifier
products.description:
The PowerPlus is the family's mid-size workhorse, listed for rooms up to 968 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour. That air-change figure is the useful one, since it comes close to the four to five changes recommended for allergy-grade cleaning in the room size it names.

It offers four cleaning levels and an auto mode, with a HEPA filter behind a carbon pre-filter, so it handles dust, dander and mild odors. The compromise is fan noise on the top level, as with any machine pushing this much air, but the lower levels are comfortable for a living room. Next to the HPA5300B it gives up some capacity for a lower cost and a smaller body.

Ownership is simple: replace the HEPA filter on schedule, wash or replace the pre-filter, and keep the intake clear. Replacement filters for the family are widely sold, which keeps it practical in year three.
products.bestFor: Medium to large bedrooms and living rooms that want a proven mid-size tower.
pros: Listed 4.8 air changes per hour near allergy standards
Four cleaning levels plus auto mode
HEPA with carbon pre-filter
Widely sold replacement filters
cons: Fan is audible on the top level
Carbon layer is modest for strong smells

products.name: Honeywell Allergen Plus HPA4300W 4-in-1 purifier
products.description:
The HPA4300W is the newest design in this group, built around an air quality sensor that drives auto mode and a filter-change system meant to keep your hands clean. The four-layer HEPA stack adds odor handling to the particle capture, aimed at homes with pets.

The LessMess approach makes swapping the filter a one-click job without touching the dirty media, a real advantage if you dislike the chore. A carry handle is built into the housing, which makes it easy to move between rooms despite the 1,718 square foot class. One catch: the sensor measures particles only, so it will not respond to gases, and the filter is proprietary.

Expect a recurring cost for the filter set. Keep the sensor window dust-free so auto mode reads accurately, and place the machine where it is not in the airflow of a vent.
products.bestFor: Households that want auto mode and a clean, easy filter swap.
pros: AQSense sensor drives auto mode
LessMess filter change avoids dirty hands
Four-layer HEPA with odor handling
Built-in carry handle
cons: Proprietary filter set adds a recurring cost

products.name: Honeywell AllergenPlus HPA304 large-room purifier
products.description:
The HPA304 is the Honeywell with the highest listed coverage in this roundup at 2,250 square feet, aimed at bedrooms and living rooms alike. It is a straightforward HEPA machine without a sensor-driven auto mode, so you set the speed yourself.

The listing carries a pointed warning that compatible filters are not comparable, and it is worth heeding: off-brand filters often do not seal against the housing, which lets air bypass the media. Genuine filters cost more but keep the machine performing at its stated level. Against the HPA3100 it covers more area, while the HPA3100 adds auto mode.

Upkeep centers on a clean pre-filter and a filter change on schedule. The white finish blends with light walls, and the manual controls make it easy to understand for anyone who dislikes electronics.
products.bestFor: Large rooms where the user prefers simple manual controls.
pros: Highest listed coverage in the Honeywell range here
Straightforward manual controls
HEPA filter with a pre-filter ahead of it
White finish blends with pale walls
cons: Genuine filters are needed for rated performance

products.name: Honeywell Air Genius 5 washable-filter purifier
products.description:
The Air Genius 5 takes a different path: its filters are permanent and washable, which removes the recurring cost of replacement cartridges. It doubles as an oscillating fan, so it earns its floor space in summer too.

The tradeoff is the filter type. Washable electrostatic media captures particles differently from a true HEPA layer, and performance drifts if the plates are not washed and dried correctly. It makes sense for owners who accept that chore and want a low-consumable machine, but it is not a substitute for a sealed HEPA unit if you are managing serious allergies.

Maintenance is a regular rinse of the filter parts and a full dry before refitting. A damp filter can smell and lose effectiveness, so set a reminder rather than relying on memory.
products.bestFor: People who would rather wash filters than keep buying them.
pros: Permanent washable filters cut consumable costs
Oscillating fan adds summer value
Five cleaning levels
Listed for up to 1,200 sq ft
cons: Not a true sealed HEPA design
Requires regular washing and full drying

products.name: Honeywell HHT270 tabletop dual-action purifier
products.description:
The HHT270 is the compact tabletop option, listed for 465 square feet in an hour and cycling the air up to 4.8 times in the room size it states. It is aimed at small rooms, offices and nurseries, where the larger machines would be oversized.

Its three power levels and simple controls keep it easy to use, but it lacks auto mode and the more elaborate sensor features of the newer designs. A dual-action filter pairs a pre-filter with a main filter, which handles dust and mild odors rather than serious allergen loads in a big space.

Upkeep is minimal: change the filter on schedule and keep the tabletop clear. If your room matches the stated size, it does honest work at a fair size.
products.bestFor: Small rooms, offices and nurseries that want a compact tabletop unit.
pros: Compact tabletop body
Listed 4.8 air changes in its stated room size
Three simple power levels
Easy to place and move

buyingCriteria.criterion: Look for air changes, not just coverage
buyingCriteria.explanation: The PowerPlus HPA3100 lists 968 square feet at 4.8 air changes per hour, a figure close to the four to five changes recommended for allergy-grade cleaning. The HPA304 lists 2,250 square feet, which almost certainly assumes fewer changes. When comparing, ask how many air changes the coverage assumes, and use a smaller room size than the box says.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Decide if you want auto mode
buyingCriteria.explanation: The HPA5300B and HPA4300W use sensors to adjust fan speed, while the HPA304 and HHT270 leave it to you. Auto mode idles on clean days and speeds up when you cook, which saves noise and electricity. Sensors only read particles, so do not expect them to react to gases or odors.

HPA models use replaceable HEPA filters with a carbon pre-filter, while the Air Genius 5 uses washable media with no recurring cost. True HEPA captures 99.97 percent of 0.3 micron particles, while washable electrostatic plates behave differently and degrade if poorly maintained. Allergy sufferers should favor the HEPA models.

The HPA304 listing warns that compatible does not mean comparable, and the warning is justified. Off-brand filters may not seal against the housing, letting air bypass the media. Genuine filters cost more per swap but keep the machine performing at its stated level, and they come with the correct gasket fit.

The HPA4300W's LessMess system makes the change a one-click job that keeps your hands off dirty media. Older designs ask you to handle the filter directly. If you dislike chores, this feature is worth paying for, since a chore you avoid becomes a filter you never replace. A purifier running on a saturated filter still hums and glows, so the failure is invisible until allergy symptoms or smells come back. Owners of the HHT270 and HPA304 should set a calendar reminder instead of trusting memory.

The carbon pre-filters on the HPA3100 and HPA5300B are light layers that soften mild smells. Heavy cooking or smoke odors need a deep carbon bed, which none of these machines carry. Treat carbon here as a helper and consider other brands if odors are the main complaint.

specDecoder.meaning: The number of times a machine cycles a room's full volume in an hour. Four to five changes is the usual target for allergy cleaning.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 4.8 changes on the HPA3100 and HHT270 apply to their stated room sizes, not bigger rooms.

specDecoder.meaning: A manufacturer estimate of the largest room the unit can serve. It is not a CADR rating and depends on the air-change assumption.
specDecoder.watchFor: The HPA304's 2,250 and HPA4300W's 1,718 should be treated as ceilings.

specDecoder.meaning: A particle sensor that changes fan speed with the air quality. It lets the fan idle when the room is clean.
specDecoder.watchFor: The sensor on the HPA4300W misses gases, so do not rely on it for odors.

specDecoder.meaning: A light carbon layer ahead of the HEPA filter that adsorbs some odors and protects the main filter.
specDecoder.watchFor: It saturates over time, so replace it on schedule on the HPA5300B and HPA3100.

specDecoder.meaning: A permanent filter cleaned with water instead of replaced. It lowers consumable costs but needs complete drying.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the Air Genius 5 uses it, and it is not equivalent to true HEPA.

howWeEvaluated.title: Air-change basis
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated coverage against the disclosed air-change rate. The HPA3100 and HHT270 name 4.8 changes per hour, which earned credit for transparency. Larger coverage numbers with no basis were discounted, because a purifier that cycles a 2,000 square foot space once an hour is doing a very different job from one that cycles 400 square feet nearly five times. We kept that distinction in every verdict.

howWeEvaluated.title: Filter system
howWeEvaluated.description: HEPA versus washable media and the presence of a carbon pre-filter were compared. The HPA models were ranked on HEPA capture, while the Air Genius 5 was judged on its lower consumable cost. Filter change design was also considered.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at auto mode, indicators and simple manual levels. The HPA5300B and HPA4300W earned credit for sensors, and the HPA304 for plain controls. All sensors were noted as particle-only.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership cost
howWeEvaluated.description: Filter price and frequency were compared using price tier data and owner feedback patterns. The Air Genius 5 saved on consumables, while genuine filters for the HPA304 and HPA5300B cost more. Availability counted in each model's favor.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and placement
howWeEvaluated.description: Footprint, carry handles and finish were reviewed against room size. The HHT270 was ranked for small rooms and the HPA5300B for large ones. Models that needed to run at maximum to serve their room were marked down. The HPA4300W's built-in carry handle counted in its favor, since a purifier that is easy to move gets used in more rooms, while the heavier floor models tend to stay in one spot for years.

maintenance.why: Hair and dust load it first. A clean pre-filter protects the HEPA layer and keeps airflow high.
The media fills with fine particles and airflow falls. A late change increases noise and lowers cleaning.
Dust on the window skews the auto mode reading. A dry cloth is enough.
Washable plates lose effectiveness when loaded. Dry fully before refitting to avoid odor.
Furniture and curtains choke airflow. Leave clear space around the unit.

faq.q: Which Honeywell is best for a bedroom?
faq.a: The HPA3100 is a sound bedroom and living room choice, with 4.8 listed air changes in its stated room size. For a smaller bedroom, the HHT270 is quieter and more compact.
They are a recurring cost, and genuine filters cost more than off-brand ones. Using genuine filters keeps the machine sealed and performing at its listed level.

faq.q: Is the Air Genius 5 as good as HEPA?
faq.a: No. Washable media behaves differently from true HEPA and degrades if not cleaned properly. It saves money on consumables but is a weaker choice for serious allergies.
Yes, it keeps the fan quiet on clean days and speeds up when the sensor detects particles. It does not detect gases, so odors may linger without a reaction from the machine.

A carbon pre-filter softens mild smells, but heavy cooking or smoke odors need a deep carbon bed. These machines suit allergens more than strong odors. If cooking smells are your main issue, place the unit near the kitchen opening and run it on a higher level while you cook and for half an hour afterward.

They are moderate on low levels and audible on high. Use auto mode where possible, and run the larger machines on lower levels for sleeping rooms, since a bigger machine on low is quieter than a small one on high.
